overview: This file traces the Japanese silk industry’s deepening depression from April 1930 through June 1932 through State Department cross-reference sheets, economic-report excerpts, a consular despatch and newspaper enclosure, and a diplomatic telegram. It documents government-backed storage and bank lending intended to support raw-silk prices, contemporary press criticism of this intervention, experiments in cheaper cocoon preservation, restrictions on Japanese experts assisting Soviet sericulture, the industry’s mounting debts and bank exposure, and the controversial sale of more than 107,000 bales of government-held silk to Paolino Gerli through the Asahi Silk Corporation. Together the documents show how an agricultural export industry became a major financial and political problem for the Japanese government during the global depression.

people.name: William R. Castle Jr.
people.role: U.S. Ambassador to Japan; author of the referenced April 1930 report

people.name: Bunjiro Miake
people.role: Professor at the Tokyo Higher Sericultural School and inventor of the Adozol Cooling System

people.name: William Cameron Forbes
people.role: U.S. Ambassador to Japan; author of the referenced February 1932 despatch

people.name: Edwin L. Neville
people.role: U.S. diplomat in Tokyo and sender or signatory of the April–June 1932 reports

people.name: Stanley K. Hornbeck

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to report no. 42 on silk prices
subfiles.about: The sheet directs researchers to report no. 42 concerning government action against the slump in Japan’s silk industry.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Castle's 1930 report on silk production curtailment, joint storage, and government support measures.

subfiles.title: Report no. 42 excerpt on government silk-price support
subfiles.about: The report explains the Japanese government’s March 1930 measures to stabilize raw-silk prices and records press opposition to them.
subfiles.summary: Report: amid near-record-low silk prices, sericulturists curtailed output and pooled storage; the government guaranteed bank losses up to ¥30 million and had the Imperial Silk Holding Company remove 50,000 bales, criticized by Tokyo papers as unwarranted favoritism.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 54 transmitting a clipping on cocoon drying
subfiles.about: Garrels transmits a Japan Advertiser article about Professor Bunjiro Miake’s new cocoon-drying system.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 54 forwards information on a new cocoon-preservation method Miake claimed could save the silk industry $100,000,000 yearly.

subfiles.title: Japan Advertiser clipping on the Adozol Cooling System
subfiles.about: The clipping describes Bunjiro Miake’s experimental cooling system for preserving cocoons and its projected savings.
subfiles.summary: Clipping: Miake's Adozol Cooling System, tested on cocoons at a Kumagaya factory, claimed lower costs, 45% greater efficiency, less storage space, and up to 20% more silk per cocoon quantity.
keywords: Katakura Silk Reeling and Spinning Company

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to despatch no. 488 on silk experts and Russia
subfiles.about: The sheet points to a despatch reporting that Japan prevented silk experts from assisting Soviet sericulture.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Forbes's despatch No. 488 on government fears that silk experts going to Russia would leak technical secrets.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 488 excerpt on silk experts and gold shipments
subfiles.about: The excerpt reports government interference with Soviet contracts for Japanese silk experts and briefly discusses Japanese gold exports.
subfiles.summary: Six Japanese silk experts contracted to assist Soviet agriculture reportedly cancelled under government pressure, fearing leaked secrets; separately, ¥89,000,000 in gold had shipped since the December 13 embargo, expected to soon cease.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to telegram no. 107 on silk-industry finance
subfiles.about: The sheet points to section D of telegram no. 107 concerning the agricultural and credit structure of Japan’s silk industry.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: silk production is primarily agricultural, with filatures borrowing from banks to finance cocoon purchases rather than holding deposits.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 107, section D, on silk-industry indebtedness
subfiles.about: The telegram estimates the Japanese silk industry’s debts, bank exposure, government liabilities, stored inventory, and depressed price level.
subfiles.summary: Neville estimates Japan's silk capital exceeds ¥250,000,000, including ¥120,000,000 lent against stored bales and ¥150,000,000 to 3,800 filatures, with potential bank losses near ¥100,000,000 and prices (¥650/bale) well below the ¥800 needed for profit.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Hornbeck memorandum on Japanese-American silk relations
subfiles.about: The sheet directs readers to a memorandum on the Japanese silk industry and its relationship with the American industry.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a Hornbeck memo on Japanese-American silk relations, filed under Dai Ichi Raw Silk Corporation records.
keywords: Dai Ichi Raw Silk Corporation of America

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to despatch no. 600 on the Gerli silk sale
subfiles.about: The sheet points to a report that the Japanese government sold a large quantity of raw silk to Paolino Gerli through the Asahi Silk Corporation.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference (May 1932) identifies Gerli, Silk Association of America president, and agent Asahi Silk Corporation in the government silk sale.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to despatch no. 634 on complications from the Gerli sale
subfiles.about: The sheet points to a June report on complications resulting from the Japanese government’s sale of silk to Paolino Gerli.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Neville's despatch No. 634 on the ongoing silk-industry crisis aggravated by the government's bulk silk sale.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 634 excerpt on the troubled aftermath of the Gerli sale
subfiles.about: The excerpt describes unresolved contractual and price-support problems following the sale of 107,850 bales of government silk.
subfiles.summary: Report: the bulk Gerli sale caused further complications rather than stabilizing silk prices, which kept falling despite secret price-support efforts, forcing the new government to decide on completing or cancelling the agreement and disposing of the silk.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 600 excerpt on the bulk sale of stored silk
subfiles.about: The excerpt reports the initial agreement to sell 107,830 bales of stored raw silk to Paolino Gerli through the Asahi Silk Corporation.
subfiles.summary: Report describes the Gerli bulk sale at ¥455 per bale, with an estimated ¥100,000,000 loss (government bearing ¥30,000,000), meant to liquidate silk accumulated amid continuing price declines after the gold embargo's restoration.

interest: Shows Japan's 1930 silk-price crisis response, cocoon-drying tech, and the disruptive 1932 Gerli silk sale.
